title: A Course In Time
pitch: A wizard trapped in a hotel that exists in two eras at once. Switch between Past and Present to open routes that exist in neither era alone.
description: Case study: A Course In Time, a 2D puzzle-metroidvania in Unity. Tyler Crump was producer and team leader, and built the era switch and playtest tooling.
contribution: Built the era switch: collision, object state and physics change in one step, and a crush check turns being caught inside a wall into a death rather than a glitch.
facts: Producer / team leader, lead playtester; also programming, level design and audio

quick.label: The game
quick.text: Switching eras changes platforms, walls and hazards. Progress is gated by abilities, not combat, across one interconnected hotel.

quick.label: My part
quick.text: Led the team through sprints and playtests. Built the era switch, the save system, player movement and the in-build debug console testers used.

quick.label: Evidence
quick.text: A released Windows build on itch.io. Three playtest sessions with 36 respondents. A final production report covering sprints 2–4.

sections.title: One building, two eras, one set of hands.
sections.intro: The hotel is the puzzle. Each era hides part of a route: a floor that has collapsed in the Present may still stand in the Past, and a wall that blocks the Past may be rubble in the Present. Progress comes from abilities, never combat.
steps: Find a path neither era allows
Unlock an ability that opens paths you could already see
abilities: Shift between Present and Past. Platforms appear, walls vanish, hazards change.
Freeze objects across both timelines; bounce beams off mirrors to hit targets around corners.
A short burst of speed to cross gaps and avoid hazards.
A second jump in mid-air to reach new areas.
Grab and move boxes into position for environmental puzzles.
sections.source: Game description and abilities from the published itch.io page.

sections.title: The era switch, reduced to one corridor.
sections.intro: This is the rule I built, cut down to a single corridor. Walk right, switch eras when a path runs out, and try switching while standing where the other era has a wall.

sections.title: What I built, and why it works that way.

items.title: Time closing around the player is a death, not a glitch
items.goal: Switching eras should read as a rule of the world that players can learn and plan around.
items.constraint: Geometry that exists in only one era can appear exactly where the player is standing at the moment they switch.
items.decision: Treat that overlap as a death, detected by a crush check, instead of pushing the player out or letting them clip through.
items.implementation: The era system swaps collision layers, object state and physics in the same step. The crush check catches the moment solid geometry from the other era would occupy the player's space.
items.effect: Standing in the wrong place when you switch always has the same outcome. It becomes something to plan around rather than a bug to report.

items.title: Saving the world's state, not just the player's position
items.goal: A reloaded game should remember which doors are open and which puzzles are done.
items.constraint: The hotel is interconnected, with shortcuts and puzzle-gated doors, so progress lives in the world, not only in where the player is standing.
items.decision: Build saving around an objective ledger: a record of completed objectives the world reads back on load.
items.implementation: The save system records objectives alongside the skill tree's save/load, so rooms restore to their solved state.
items.effect: Coming back to the game doesn't mean re-solving rooms or finding shortcuts locked again.

items.title: A debug console in the playtest build
items.goal: Playtesters and teammates need to reach and repeat any situation quickly.
items.constraint: Playtests run on builds, not in the Unity editor, and progression is gated by abilities, so late rooms normally take a full playthrough to reach.
items.decision: Ship playtest builds with an in-build console instead of relying on editor-only shortcuts.
items.implementation: Noclip, ability grants, scene jumps and objective control, all available without the editor.
items.effect: Testers can jump straight to the room being tested instead of replaying the game to reach it.

sections.title: Systems and tools I built.
sections.intro: Programming was shared with the team; Payton Saunders was lead programmer. These are the parts I built.
items: The era system: collision layers, object state and physics swapped in step, with the crush check.
Moving-platform passenger behaviour, player dash and jump, and player audio.
A skill tree with save/load, the objective-ledger save system and the HUD.
Procedural puzzle generators with Scene-view grid painting. Pipe networks use a connectivity solver. Elemental puzzles choose their elements by counting how many valid solutions each set allows.
The in-build debug console for playtesters.
WebGL audio compatibility fixes and URP particle shaders.

sections.title: Running the team and the tests.
items: Led sprint planning, workload coordination and retrospectives for the five-person team.
Designed and ran three playtest sessions with 36 respondents in total, and analysed the feedback to guide iteration.
Wrote the final production report for sprints 2–4, covering workload, retrospectives and goal tracking.
An earlier plan had three eras. The current build has two: Past and Present.
sections.gap: The findings from those sessions, and the specific changes they led to, aren't written up here yet.
